notes.b: Volumetric analysis uses a measured volume of reaction to find an unknown concentration.
points: Volumetric analysis (titration) finds the concentration of a solution, the analyte, by measuring the volume that reacts exactly with a known volume of another solution of known concentration.
The calculation depends on knowing one concentration exactly, so at least one of the two solutions must be a standard solution.
Titre: the volume of solution added from the burette.
End point: the point at which the indicator changes colour.
Equivalence point: the point at which the reactants have reacted in exactly the mole ratio of the balanced equation.
A good indicator is one whose end point coincides with the equivalence point.
A primary standard is a very pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed accurately and dissolved to give a standard solution directly.
Its properties and the method for making up a standard solution are covered in “Solutions and concentration”.
Acid–base primary standard: anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃.
Redox primary standard: ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O.
Every result in volumetric analysis is only as accurate as the standard: an impure or unstable standard gives a wrong concentration, and so a wrong answer for the analyte.

notes.b: Some reagents cannot be made up directly as standard solutions, so their concentration must be found by titration.
points: Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air.
Potassium manganate(VII) solution slowly decomposes, especially in light and in the presence of organic matter, forming MnO₂.
Sodium thiosulfate crystals have an uncertain water content.
Standardisation is finding the exact concentration of such a solution by titrating it against a primary standard, or against a solution already standardised against one.
Example: hydrochloric acid is standardised by titration against a standard solution of sodium carbonate: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Example: sodium hydroxide is then standardised against the standardised hydrochloric acid, and potassium manganate(VII) is standardised against ammonium iron(II) sulfate.
A solution standardised in this way is sometimes called a secondary standard.

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of a primary standard in volumetric analysis and name one primary standard used in acid–base titrations.
questions.model: Volumetric analysis finds the concentration of an analyte from the volume that reacts with a known volume of another solution, so at least one of the two solutions must be a standard solution whose concentration is known exactly. A primary standard is a very pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed accurately and dissolved to give a standard solution directly. Its importance is that every result is only as accurate as the standard: an impure or unstable standard gives a wrong concentration and therefore a wrong answer for the analyte. One primary standard used in acid–base titrations is anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃.

questions.prompt: What is meant by standardising a solution? Explain why hydrochloric acid must be standardised before it is used in a titration.
questions.model: Standardising a solution is finding its exact concentration by titrating it against a primary standard, or against a solution already standardised against one. Hydrochloric acid must be standardised because it is volatile, so it cannot be made up directly as a standard solution and its concentration is not known exactly. It is therefore titrated against a standard solution of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), and the exact concentration found is then used in later titrations.
